name: Pierre Louÿs
bio: French poet and novelist (1870-1925). He founded the review La Conque in 1889, at nineteen, and printed Swinburne, Verlaine, Mallarmé, Maeterlinck, Gide and Moréas in it. He met Wilde in Paris in November 1891, went over the French of Salomé line by line, and Wilde dedicated the play to him - 'À mon ami Pierre Louÿs', his name, as Wilde put it, written in gold on purple. Fifteen months later the friendship was over. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive and they hold the whole arc, from 'Cher Monsieur Louÿs' to 'Mon très cher Ennemi' to the last one, which ends: 'It is new to me to think that friendship is more brittle than love is.'
bio_note: Seven letters; four read (printed 496, 506, 528, 557) Dates 1870-1925 from the editors' note at printed 496.

sources.quote: Cher Monsieur Louÿs, J'accepte avec le plus vif plaisir la gracieuse et charmante invitation que vous et M. Gide ont eu la bonté de m'adresser. Vous m'indiquerez, n'est-ce-pas, l'endroit et l'heure.
sources.translation: Dear Monsieur Louÿs, I accept with the keenest pleasure the gracious and charming invitation which you and M. Gide have been kind enough to address to me. You will tell me, will you not, the place and the hour.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, 28 November 1891, 29 boulevard des Capucines - the first of the five, quoted whole. Wilde was thirty-seven, Louÿs twenty-one. The invitation came from two people. The editors note that André Gide had met Wilde for the first time the day before, on 27 November, and wrote to Paul Valéry about him that same week; that according to his letters he then saw Wilde almost every day until 15 December; and that the pages of his journal covering those days have been torn out. Gide is not on this map and should be.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The opening of the friendship, and the fact that Gide was there from the first day of it.

sources.quote: Mon cher ami, Voilà le drame de Salomé. Ce n'est pas encore fini ou même corrigé, mais ça donne l'idée de la construction, du motif et du mouvement dramatique. Ici et là, il y a des lacunes, mais l'idée du dráme est claire.
sources.translation: My dear friend, Here is the drama of Salomé. It is not yet finished or even corrected, but it gives the idea of the construction, of the motif and of the dramatic movement. Here and there, there are gaps, but the idea of the drama is clear.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [December 1891], Paris (MS Clark) - quoted whole, and the address has moved to 'mon cher ami'. This is Wilde handing over the manuscript of Salomé; the editors identify the draft as the third and apparently final one, which carries Louÿs's interlinear corrections. Where the corrections were points of grammar Wilde took them, and most of the rest he deleted or ignored.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The collaboration the dedication was payment for.

sources.quote: Mon très cher Ennemi, Pourquoi pas d'adresse sur ta carte? Voilà deux jours que je te cherche!! Enfin, voulez-vous diner avec moi ce soir? Rendez-vous Café Royal, Regent Street, 7.45, habit de matin. Je serai charmé naturellement si Madame vous accompagne. Et j'inviterai John Gray.
sources.translation: My very dear Enemy, Why no address on your card? I have been looking for you these two days!! Well then, will you dine with me this evening? Meet at the Café Royal, Regent Street, 7.45, morning dress. I shall be charmed naturally if Madame accompanies you. And I shall invite John Gray.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [June 1892], on Louÿs's first visit to London - quoted whole. Note the pronouns: Wilde opens with the intimate 'ta carte' and 'je te cherche', then switches to the formal 'voulez-vous' for the invitation itself, which is either affection catching itself or the reverse. The 'Madame' is Lucile Delormet, the young woman Louÿs came to London with. John Gray is on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship at its most familiar - a joke address, two days of looking, and John Gray asked along.

sources.quote: My dear Pierre, Is the enclosed really all that you have to say to me in return for my choosing you out of all my friends to whom to dedicate Salomé? I cannot tell you how hurt I am. Those to whom I merely gave copies have written me charming letters coloured with delicate appreciation of my work. You alone - you whose name I have written in gold on purple - you say nothing, and I don't understand what your telegram means; some trivial jest I suppose; a drop of froth without wine. How you disappoint me! Had you wired 'Je vous remercie' it would have been enough. It is new to me to think that friendship is more brittle than love is.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [postmark 27 February 1893], Torquay - the last of the five, quoted whole, and written in English, which none of the others are. Salomé had been published in Paris the previous week, dedicated 'À mon ami Pierre Louÿs'; Louÿs had answered with a telegram Wilde could not read the tone of. The friendship did not recover. The closing sentence is as near as Wilde comes anywhere in this volume to saying what he thought friendship was, and he says it at the moment of losing one.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The end of it, in Wilde's own hand, and the sentence the whole node is for.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Lane, Here is your seat; front row of dress-circle; I think the best in the house. Next you, you will find Pierre Louÿs, the young poet to whom I dedicated Salomé. Pray introduce yourself to him. He is a perfect English scholar. In haste
sources.context: Wilde to John Lane, [? 19 April 1893], Hotel Albemarle - the first night of A Woman of No Importance, quoted whole. It complicates the break, which is why it is here: this is seven weeks after the letter saying friendship is more brittle than love, and Wilde has given Louÿs a front-row seat, seated a publisher beside him and told the publisher to introduce himself. Whatever ended between them had not ended by that evening, or had not finished ending.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the break was not clean, and that Wilde was still placing him well seven weeks later.
